turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hello, Doctor. I... well, I came in because ever since my wife’s fall, things have just sort of fallen apart for me. 

I’ve always been the man with the lists and the plan. I handle things. But lately, I just find myself sitting at the kitchen table, staring at her medication chart. I'll start crying, or I'll snap over absolutely nothing. And everything else is just piling up—the bills, my mentoring calls, even just basic housework. It’s like I just... I can’t make myself function anymore.

symptom_reasoning.S081: The patient reports significant emotional distress (crying, snapping) and functional impairment (inability to handle chores, bills, or mentoring) occurring directly in response to an identifiable stressor (his wife's fall).

turns.doctor_question: When your wife had her fall, how long ago was that, and when did you first notice these changes in yourself—the crying, the irritability, and difficulty with tasks?
turns.patient_response:
Her fall was only about two months ago. As for the changes in me... well, it didn't happen right away. 

I certainly didn't have any of these issues before she got hurt. But even right after it happened, I was mostly just focused on getting her through the hospital stay. It was really after we got home and the whole daily caregiving routine took over. Once I became the one responsible for managing all her physical needs and her schedule... that's when I started falling apart.

symptom_reasoning.S081: The patient confirms that their emotional distress and decompensation ('falling apart') developed specifically in response to an identifiable stressor (his wife's fall and subsequent caregiving burdens two months ago).

turns.doctor_question: Besides the crying and irritability, have you noticed changes in your sleep, appetite, or energy levels over these past weeks?
turns.patient_response: I haven't really noticed any major changes there, to be honest. I mean, my energy is maybe a little low just from the stress of it all, but I'm still sleeping through the night fine. And my appetite is pretty much the same as it's always been. I haven't lost any weight or anything like that.

symptom_reasoning.S026: The patient explicitly denies appetite or weight changes, stating their appetite is normal and they haven't lost weight.
symptom_reasoning.S027: The patient explicitly denies sleep problems, reporting that they are still sleeping through the night fine.

turns.doctor_question: Beyond the crying and irritability, have you done anything during this time that you normally wouldn't do—like lashing out at your wife, neglecting her care, spending money recklessly, or acting in ways that go against your values?
turns.patient_response: No, no, nothing like that. I would never neglect her care or lash out at her. She's the one who's hurt, you know? It's not her fault. And I haven't been doing anything reckless or... out of character in that way. No spending sprees or anything. It's just the crying and getting frustrated over little things, mostly with myself or the situation, not with her.

symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient confirms experiencing crying spells (tearfulness).
symptom_reasoning.S060: The patient reports getting frustrated over minor things, demonstrating low frustration tolerance.
symptom_reasoning.S041: The patient explicitly denies engaging in reckless behaviors or spending sprees.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned getting frustrated over little things—when you snap or feel irritable, have you done anything during those moments that you later regret, like raising your voice harshly at your wife, throwing or breaking things, or acting in ways that surprised you?
turns.patient_response:
No, I haven't... I haven't done anything like that. When I say I get frustrated, it's more of an internal thing, or I might just mutter under my breath. 

I haven't raised my voice at my wife, and I certainly haven't thrown or broken anything. If I feel myself getting short-tempered, I usually just step into the other room for a minute to collect myself. The irritability is definitely there, and it's exhausting, but I haven't acted out aggressively or done anything that I'd regret like that.

symptom_reasoning.S077: The patient explicitly denies verbal or physical aggression, confirming they have never raised their voice, thrown or broken items, or acted out aggressively.

turns.doctor_question: Since your wife's fall, have you done anything that violated rules or the rights of others—for example, breaking agreements you'd normally keep, acting dishonestly, or doing something that could get you into trouble with others or the law?
turns.patient_response: No, nothing like that at all. I haven't broken any rules or done anything dishonest. I'm just... I'm just trying to get through the days and take care of my wife. I certainly haven't done anything that would get me into trouble.

turns.doctor_question: Since your wife's fall, have you done anything—even small things—that goes against what you normally believe is right, or that you know other people wouldn't approve of? For example, have you been neglecting any responsibilities you usually take seriously, or acting in ways that don't match your values?
turns.patient_response: Well, I suppose I have been neglecting some responsibilities. I used to be very involved in my community—mentoring young folks, showing up for committee meetings—but I've completely stopped going. I just don't have the energy for it right now. And even around the house, things I used to handle without a second thought are slipping badly. I'm falling behind on paying the bills, the yard work is piling up, and just keeping up with the basic household routines feels impossible lately. I know I should be doing these things, and it bothers me that I'm not, but I just can't seem to manage it all right now.

turns.doctor_question: When your wife first came home from the hospital after her fall, did you start experiencing the crying and irritability right away, or was there a gap of several days or more before these symptoms began?
turns.patient_response: Well, it wasn't right away. Her fall was only about two months ago... and at first, I was just focused on getting her home and settled. I think the crying and the irritability started a bit later, maybe after a few weeks. It really started happening after the daily caregiving routine took over and the reality of it all set in. I didn't feel like this before that routine started.

turns.doctor_question: When you say the crying and irritability started 'a bit later' after the caregiving routine took over, can you be more specific about the timing? Was it within the first few days after your wife came home, or was it more like a week or two later?
turns.patient_response: It was probably more like a week or two later. Like I said, her fall was only about two months ago total, so it all still feels pretty recent. But I was holding it together at first. I didn't start falling apart before the caregiving routine took over. The first few days she was home, I was just focused on getting her settled and making sure she was safe. It was only after that heavy, daily routine really became our reality that I started breaking down, definitely not before it.

symptom_reasoning.S081: The patient confirms that their emotional breakdown occurred a week or two after their wife's fall and subsequent caregiving routine began, clearly linking their symptoms to an identifiable stressor.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned the crying and irritability started about a week or two after your wife came home. Well, I'm not sure I'd use the word 'normal,' given the circumstances. It was obviously a very stressful time. But... no, I wasn't crying, and I wasn't irritable yet. 

I was just running on adrenaline, I suppose. I was entirely focused on getting her settled and figuring out the immediate logistics of having her back in the house. The emotional part—the crying and feeling so on edge all the time—that definitely didn't happen in those first few days.

turns.doctor_question: When you say the crying and irritability started about a week or two after your wife came home, do you mean it was closer to around 3-4 days, or was it definitely more like 7-14 days after she arrived home?

I really couldn't give you an exact number of days. It all kind of... blurs together, to be honest.

I just know it wasn't right at the very beginning. It just sort of crept up on me once the adrenaline wore off and the reality of the daily care really set in.
